concept.name: Key-Value Store Patterns

relationships.description: Connects Key-Value Store Patterns to database indexing in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Key-value stores trade relational joins and ad-hoc secondary queries for O(1) or O(log N) lookups partitioned by a primary key across memory or LSM-trees.
spark.keyTakeaway: Design keys around your exact read access pattern first—composite keys, hash tags, and TTLs replace SQL joins, while hot-key sharding and compaction tuning prevent tail-latency spikes.

concept.whyItMatters: Modern high-throughput services—session stores, feature flags, rate limiters, and metadata catalogs—need sub-millisecond reads and predictable horizontal scaling that B-tree RDBMS engines struggle to sustain past 100k+ QPS. Choosing the right key-value engine (in-memory hash vs. disk-backed LSM-tree) and key-modeling pattern determines whether your p99 stays under 2 ms or collapses under hot partitions and write amplification.
whenToUse: Point lookups and writes indexed by a known primary identifier (userId, sessionId, idempotencyKey) at 10k–1M+ ops/sec.
Ephemeral or TTL-bound state such as JWT blocklists, distributed locks (Redlock/etcd leases), and sliding-window rate-limit counters.
Write-heavy ingestion (telemetry, time-series buckets, event deduplication) where append-only LSM-trees (RocksDB, DynamoDB) outperform random B-tree page writes.
whenNotToUse: Multi-attribute ad-hoc filtering, range aggregations across arbitrary columns, or multi-table joins—use PostgreSQL or ClickHouse instead.
Strict multi-entity ACID transactions spanning uncorrelated keys across shards without accepting 2PC latency penalties.
Large binary blobs (>1 MB) in memory-first engines like Redis or Memcached, which fragment slab allocators and starve working-set RAM.
keyPoints: Access-pattern-driven key naming: encode hierarchy and cardinality in keys (e.g., tenant:{id}:session:{sid}) and use Redis hash tags ({tenant:42}:cart) to co-locate multi-key operations on the same hash slot.

Storage engine split: in-memory hash tables (Redis, Memcached) deliver <1 ms p99 at RAM cost, while LSM-trees (RocksDB, Pebble) buffer writes in a MemTable + WAL and flush immutable SSTables for high write throughput on NVMe.

Partitioning & consistent hashing: Redis Cluster maps keys to 16,384 hash slots via CRC16(key) mod 16384; DynamoDB hashes the partition key (PK) into storage partitions capped at 1,000 WCU / 3,000 RCU per physical partition.

Value serialization & compression: packing small related attributes into a single Hash or Protobuf/MessagePack blob cuts per-key metadata overhead (~64–96 bytes per Redis key) and reduces network round-trips.

Read/write amplification defenses: 10-bit/key Bloom filters (~1% false positive rate) skip non-existent SSTable lookups, while leveled compaction bounds space amplification to ~1.1x at the cost of ~10x write amplification.

examples.title: Flash-Sale Inventory & Idempotency in Redis Cluster
examples.scenario: An e-commerce checkout service handles 80,000 RPS during a flash sale and must atomically decrement SKU stock while preventing duplicate charges from client retries.
examples.outcome: Using hash-tagged keys ({sku:991}:stock and {sku:991}:idem:{reqId}) keeps both keys on the same Redis Cluster slot, enabling a single-round-trip Lua script to check idempotency, decrement stock, and set a 24h TTL in 0.6 ms p99.

examples.title: Multi-Tenant Feature Store on DynamoDB
examples.scenario: A personalization API fetches 50 user-level ML features per request with a 15 ms SLA and 40 TB of total feature history.
examples.outcome: Modeling PK=user#{id} and SK=feat#{namespace} groups all features for a user into one contiguous B-tree/SSTable range, allowing a single Query call (up to 1 MB) to replace 50 GetItem calls and cut DynamoDB RCU spend by 72%.

tradeOffs.pro: Redis serves reads/writes in 0.2–0.8 ms with zero disk seeks and native data structures (Sorted Sets, HyperLogLog).
tradeOffs.con: RAM costs ~10–20x more per GB than NVMe SSD, and RDB/AOF fork snapshots can double memory usage during copy-on-write spikes.

tradeOffs.factor: Composite Key Packing vs. Normalized Single-Attribute Keys
tradeOffs.pro: Packing 10 attributes into one Hash or Protobuf value eliminates 9 network hops and saves ~700 bytes of key-header overhead per entity.
tradeOffs.con: Updating a single 8-byte field in a serialized blob requires a read-modify-write cycle (or CAS) and rewrites the entire value.

tradeOffs.pro: Leveled compaction keeps space amplification near 1.1x and bounds point-read checks to one SSTable per level.
tradeOffs.con: Write amplification reaches 10–30x on heavy update workloads, saturating NVMe IOPS and causing compaction stalls.

failureModes.name: Hot-Key Partition Saturation
failureModes.description: A single celebrity key or global counter hashes to one shard, maxing out its single-threaded CPU (Redis) or 3,000 RCU/1,000 WCU partition ceiling (DynamoDB) while other shards sit idle.
failureModes.mitigation: Apply write sharding by appending a random suffix (counter#0..counter#15) and aggregating on read, or place a 1–5 second L1 in-process cache (Caffeine/Ristretto) in front of hot read keys.

failureModes.name: Cache Stampede / Thundering Herd on Expiry
failureModes.description: A popular key expires simultaneously across 500 app pods, triggering 500 concurrent origin database queries that exhaust connection pools.
failureModes.mitigation: Add ±15% TTL jitter, use singleflight request coalescing per pod, or serve stale values while refreshing asynchronously in the background (stale-while-revalidate).

failureModes.name: Big-Key Blocking & Replication Lag
failureModes.description: A single 50 MB Hash or List blocks Redis's single-threaded event loop during DEL, HGETALL, or serialization, spiking p99 latency across all tenants.
failureModes.mitigation: Cap collection sizes (<10,000 elements), shard large lists into time/index buckets, and always use UNLINK (async lazyfree) instead of synchronous DEL.

failureModes.name: LSM Compaction Write Stall
failureModes.description: Sustained write bursts fill L0 SSTables faster than background compaction threads can merge them into L1, causing RocksDB to throttle or halt client writes.
failureModes.mitigation: Increase max_background_jobs, tune level0_slowdown_writes_trigger (e.g., 20) vs. stop_writes_trigger (36), and rate-limit bulk backfills.

commonMistakes: Running KEYS * or unbounded HGETALL in production Redis instead of cursor-based SCAN/HSCAN, stalling the single-threaded event loop.
Using sequential or low-cardinality partition keys (e.g., status='ACTIVE' or today's date) in distributed KV stores, funnelling 100% of traffic onto one node.
Omitting TTLs on session, cache, or idempotency keys, causing unbounded memory growth until OOM eviction drops critical keys.
Assuming multi-key MGET or Lua scripts work across Redis Cluster nodes without {hash_tag} co-location, triggering CROSSSLOT errors.
Storing unindexed JSON strings when only 1–2 fields are queried, forcing full payload deserialization on every read.

sections.content:
## The idea

A key-value store is an associative array scaled across processes and machines: given an opaque key $K$, it locates the owning partition in $O(1)$ via consistent hashing or a range/slot map, then resolves $K \to V$ locally using either an in-memory hash table (e.g., Redis `dict`, Memcached slabbed hash) or a disk-backed Log-Structured Merge-tree (e.g., RocksDB, DynamoDB storage nodes). Because the engine refuses to parse or join across arbitrary value fields, it eliminates query-planner overhead, lock-manager contention across tables, and random B-tree page splits—delivering predictable single-digit millisecond latency as data scales from gigabytes to petabytes.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider writing and reading `user:84920:prefs` in a RocksDB-backed KV node:
1. **Routing**: The client hashes `user:84920` via MurmurHash3 or CRC16 to select Shard 7 (Raft leader).
2. **Durable Write**: The node appends the mutation to an on-disk Write-Ahead Log (WAL) with `fdatasync` and inserts it into the in-memory `MemTable` (skip list) in ~80 µs.
3. **Flush**: Once the `MemTable` hits 64 MB, it freezes into an immutable `MemTable` and flushes sequentially to an L0 `SSTable` file on NVMe.
4. **Read Path**: A `Get(user:84920:prefs)` checks the active `MemTable`, immutable `MemTables`, and then L0→Ln SSTables. Each SSTable's 10-bit/key Bloom filter (~1% false positive rate) immediately skips files that do not contain the key, avoiding unnecessary disk I/O.

sections.content:
## Key Modeling & Partitioning Patterns

Effective KV schemas encode relationships directly into keys:
- **Composite / Hierarchical Keys**: `<entity>:<id>:<subresource>` (e.g., `org:42:invoice:2026-11`) enables prefix range scans in ordered engines (RocksDB, DynamoDB SK `begins_with`) without secondary indexes.
- **Hash-Tag Co-location**: In Redis Cluster, wrapping the shard root in braces (`{org:42}:quota` and `{org:42}:users`) forces CRC16 to hash only `org:42`, guaranteeing both keys land on the same slot for atomic Lua or `MGET`.
- **Write-Sharded Counters**: For hot keys exceeding 1,000 WCU or single-core limits, split into `likes:post99#0` through `likes:post99#15` on write and sum 16 keys on read.
- **Inverted Index / Adjacency Lists**: Store `tag:distributed -> Set[docId]` or `edge:nodeA -> SortedSet(ts, nodeB)` when bounded cardinality (<10k items) replaces an RDBMS join table.

## Engine & Pattern Comparison

| Pattern / Engine | Data Structure | Typical p99 Latency | Max Value Practical Limit | Primary Failure Mode |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Redis (RESP3 / Cluster)** | In-memory hash + skip list (`zset`) | 0.3–1.0 ms | ~512 MB (keep <100 KB) | Big-key event-loop stall / OOM |
| **RocksDB / Pebble** | LSM-tree (MemTable + SSTable) | 1.5–6.0 ms (NVMe) | Tens of MB (prefer <1 MB) | L0 compaction write stall |
| **Amazon DynamoDB** | Partitioned B-tree / LSM hybrid | 3–10 ms | 400 KB hard cap | Hot partition 1k WCU / 3k RCU cap |
| **etcd (v3)** | Raft + bbolt (CoW B+tree) | 2–8 ms (quorum) | 1.5 MB default request cap | MVCC revision bloat without compaction |
| **Memcached** | Slab-allocated hash table | 0.2–0.6 ms | 1 MB default slab cap | Slab calcification on shifting value sizes |

## Failure modes

1. **Hot-Key Skew**: Consistent hashing balances key count, not traffic volume. A single viral key can saturate one shard's CPU or NIC while 99% of the cluster is idle.
2. **Tombstone Accumulation**: Deleting millions of keys in an LSM-tree writes tombstone markers rather than freeing bytes immediately; range scans over deleted prefixes (`Seek`) degrade to $O(T)$ until compaction purges them.
3. **Thundering Herd on Expiration**: Synchronized TTLs cause simultaneous cache misses across all application replicas, overwhelming downstream databases.
4. **Split-Brain & Stale Reads**: Async replication (e.g., Redis primary→replica) can lose acknowledged writes during a primary crash (`WAIT` only blocks best-effort unless synchronous quorum like Raft/etcd is used).

## Serialization, TTLs & Memory Efficiency

Every standalone key in Redis carries ~64–96 bytes of metadata (`redisObject`, `dictEntry`, SDS header). Packing 100 small counters or attributes into a single `Hash` (with `hash-max-listpack-entries 512`) or a Zstd-compressed Protobuf blob cuts RAM usage by 4–8x. Always attach randomized TTL jitter (`base_ttl + rand(0, 0.15 * base_ttl)`) to prevent synchronized expiry waves, and prefer `UNLINK` over `DEL` for any value larger than 4 KB so memory reclamation runs on a background thread.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Document every read/write access pattern before choosing a key format or partition key.
- [ ] Verify partition-key cardinality is high enough to distribute peak QPS across all shards (no date-only or status-only PKs).
- [ ] Add ±10–15% jitter to all cache TTLs and use `singleflight` on cache-miss origin fetches.
- [ ] Cap collection sizes (<10k items) or chunk them into numbered buckets; use `UNLINK` and `SCAN` instead of `DEL` and `KEYS`.
- [ ] Enable 10-bit/key Bloom filters and monitor L0 file count / compaction pending bytes on LSM-backed stores.
- [ ] Use `{hash_tag}` in Redis Cluster for any multi-key Lua script or `MGET`.

interviewProblems.title: Key-Value Store Patterns
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Key-Value Store Patterns. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

simulation.title: Interactive Simulation: Key Value Store Patterns

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Key-value stores trade relational joins and ad-hoc secondary queries for O(1) or O(log N) lookups partitioned by a primary key across memory or LSM-trees.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: L0–Ln SSTables applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Bloom & Block Cache.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Bloom & Block Cache experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Apply write sharding by appending a random suffix (counter#0..counter#15) and aggregating on read, or place a 1–5 second L1 in-process cache (Caffeine/Ristretto) in front of hot read keys.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Design keys around your exact read access pattern first—composite keys, hash tags, and TTLs replace SQL joins, while hot-key sharding and compaction tuning prevent tail-latency spikes.
Avoid trap: Running KEYS * or unbounded HGETALL in production Redis instead of cursor-based SCAN/HSCAN, stalling the single-threaded event loop.
Avoid trap: Using sequential or low-cardinality partition keys (e.g., status='ACTIVE' or today's date) in distributed KV stores, funnelling 100% of traffic onto one node.
When to reach for it: Point lookups and writes indexed by a known primary identifier (userId, sessionId, idempotencyKey) at 10k–1M+ ops/sec.
When to reach for it: Ephemeral or TTL-bound state such as JWT blocklists, distributed locks (Redlock/etcd leases), and sliding-window rate-limit counters.

putItTogether.title: Putting Key Value Store Patterns Together
putItTogether.summary: Design keys around your exact read access pattern first—composite keys, hash tags, and TTLs replace SQL joins, while hot-key sharding and compaction tuning prevent tail-latency spikes.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Key Value Store Patterns before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Using hash-tagged keys ({sku:991}:stock and {sku:991}:idem:{reqId}) keeps both keys on the same Redis Cluster slot, enabling a single-round-trip Lua script to check idempotency, decrement stock, and set a 24h TTL in 0.6 ms p99.
